title: Show HN: AI scientist builds an open-source Codex Micro from scratch for $40
text:
A few weeks ago, we open-sourced our design for a cost-effective but full featured alternative to OpenAI x Work Louder's sold out Codex Micro macropad. And now, we're pleased to share that we've actually built them and they work!

Quick recap of the I/O: - 13 assignable keys with individual LEDs - rotary encoder - joystick - touch disc - optional edge-lit LED band

The cool part for us was just HOW our agent was able to do it when every other agentic skills, tools, and even commercial platforms failed. We put together a more detailed writeup in the linked blog post (plus pretty pictures!), but long story short, we asked our agentic scientist, Marvin, to treat the electrical engineering as a research problem.

Marvin was able to synthesize vast technical documents and best practice guidelines (e.g. scientific literature), test specific placement and routing strategies (e.g. experiments), and selectively backtrack and combine learnings (e.g. interpreting data analysis). The end result was a fully routed board (made especially challenging by some hard constraints to keep cost down) plus a reusable runbook worfklow that demonstrated Marvin's ability to enter an unfamiliar domain, learn and improve through experimentation, and unlock novel capabilities.

Some future work we've got marinating in our mind grapes: - an app for cross coding agent compatibility (shoutout to lop1381997 for contributing a codex-native firmware) - optional OLED screen, something like an SSD1306 that could fit right into the space between the knob and joystick - optional base with bluetooth and battery for full wireless functionality

Let us know what you think, have any ideas or feature requests, and share pictures if you build it!

title: Show HN: Llmcanvas.chat Tree-based LLM chat on an infinite canvas
text:
No one thinks linearly, yet current LLM interfaces still force you to, and it sucks.

So I built llmcanvas.chat. The name says it all; you can branch, regenerate across models and compare: all in one infinite canvas.

Every prompt and response is a node in the canvas and it brings ultimate flexibility on how you interact with the LLM, while keeping the old-school way of chatting linearly.

Bring your own keys, 4 providers supported: Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, and OpenRouter.

Try it: llmcanvas.chat. I'd love to hear your feedback.

title: Re: Ramp Built Inspect...
text:
I think the more coding agents the better, more ideas mixing and borrowing that’s yielding improvements across actively developed agents and different tradeoffs being made. From the article, Ramp’s Inspect was made with frontend in mind and is particularly good with Ramp internal tooling. Looks like it’s not open source? https://inspect.ramp.engineering/auth/

The blog post doesn’t have much further material or at least not before the paid envelope.

Some thoughts I have -

> 1. Local machines are limited in how many agents they can run. Ramp found third-party products below expectations; they liked Claude Code on day 1, but were constrained by only being able to run one or two sessions on local machines.

I haven’t seen this constraint? I only started using Claude Code ~4 months ago so maybe it was different before.

> 3. Need for remote dev environments. As Ramp scaled, so did the complexity, and with it there was more work at the intersection of systems, like debugging backward compatibility, and broken API contracts. The solution was to create remote dev environments.

This seems disjoint, not sure I follow how remote dev environments was necessary to solve this or why remote dev environments would be the only solution?

> Hooking up Inspect to the data sources that engineers would browse with the same tools seems to be a key difference between Inspect and third-party AI harnesses.

You can do the same with third party AI harnesses, I guess we’d have to see what Inspect does that’s better than providing MCPs, CLIs, scripts, etc. to an agent.

title: Re: Bill Gates: The turbulent AI era is here...
text:
> In the United States, I’ve met families who, understandably, were overwhelmed by the process of applying for health insurance, student aid, or food assistance. Faced with a huge stack of complicated bureaucratic forms, many felt like giving up. AI can streamline things dramatically

I'd love to see anyone building Grokbot or ChatGPT Work talk about how they're thinking about this use case, specifically. It seems greatly important and tractable given how little government websites & forms change over time.

On the other end - yes, it will create massive vectors for abuse & fraud, since govt services are designed to have roadblocks to reduce usage. But fraud has always been possible, even without AI (so many recent examples to pull from).

IMO it's best to maximize social benefits to see where the tradeoffs really are. We won't know until we push on it!
